introduction-the-problem-of-agreement.core: Consensus is getting a group of nodes to agree on a value (or an ordered log of values) despite crashes and message delays, so the group acts like one reliable machine. It underpins leader election, replicated state machines, configuration stores (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul) and distributed databases. Safety (never disagree) and liveness (eventually decide) are the two requirements.

first_principles.problem: Three database replicas each accept different writes during a network glitch and end up with conflicting data.
truths: Nodes crash and messages are delayed.
A replicated log makes many machines act as one.
derivation: Require **safety**: no two nodes decide differently.

analogy.title: A committee voting on minutes
analogy.story: Members may be absent or late, but the official minutes must never contain contradictory decisions.
analogy.breaks: Committees can wait for latecomers indefinitely; systems need timeouts to stay live.

example.title: Replicated state machine
flow: Leader appends to log, replicates to followers
All apply in log order → identical state

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Three machines behave like one reliable one.

check.q: What are the two core properties a consensus algorithm must provide?
check.a: Safety (never decide conflicting values) and liveness (eventually decide).

the-flp-impossibility-and-why-it-matters.core: The FLP result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985) proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus in a fully asynchronous system if even one process may crash, because you can't distinguish a crashed node from a slow one. Practical algorithms keep safety always and achieve liveness using timeouts and partial synchrony assumptions (or randomisation).

first_principles.problem: Engineers expect a consensus system to always make progress during severe network instability.
truths: Slow and dead are indistinguishable without time bounds.
derivation: Accept **FLP**: no guaranteed liveness in pure asynchrony.

analogy.title: Waiting for a friend who might have left
analogy.story: You can never be sure they're not just running late, so you pick a time to stop waiting.
analogy.breaks: Friends can phone; nodes may be unreachable entirely during partitions.

branches.label: Result
children: No deterministic guaranteed consensus with one crash in async

example.title: Raft and FLP
flow: Network chaos → elections keep timing out

check.q: What does the FLP impossibility result say?
check.a: In a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination if even one process may crash.

the-core-concept-quorums.core: A quorum is a subset of nodes whose agreement is required for an action. With majority quorums (⌊n/2⌋+1), any two quorums overlap in at least one node, so a new decision always 'sees' the previous one. That overlap is what prevents split-brain. More generally, read quorum R and write quorum W must satisfy R + W > N for reads to see the latest write.

first_principles.problem: A 4-node cluster splits 2–2 and both halves accept writes.
truths: Even splits can't both have majorities.

analogy.title: A board requiring a majority vote
analogy.story: Two different majorities must share at least one member, who remembers what was decided before.
analogy.breaks: Board members remember everything; nodes rely on persisted logs.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Even sizes add cost, not tolerance.

check.q: Why don't 4-node consensus clusters tolerate more failures than 3-node ones?
check.a: A 4-node majority is 3, so it still tolerates only one failure, like a 3-node cluster.

paxos-the-pioneer.core: Paxos (Lamport) reaches agreement in two phases. In Prepare/Promise, a proposer picks a ballot number and asks acceptors to promise not to accept lower ballots, learning any value already accepted. In Accept/Accepted, it proposes the highest previously accepted value (or its own) and is chosen once a majority accepts. Multi-Paxos elects a stable leader to skip phase 1 for a sequence of log entries.

first_principles.problem: Two proposers propose different values concurrently, and the system must choose exactly one.
truths: Previously accepted values must be preserved.
derivation: **Phase 2**: accept(n, v) with v = highest seen or own.

analogy.title: Reserving a meeting room with numbered requests
analogy.story: Higher-numbered requests override older ones, but if a booking was already nearly confirmed, you must honour it.
analogy.breaks: Room managers are central; Paxos acceptors are many and independent.

check.q: Why must a Paxos proposer adopt the highest-numbered value it learns in phase 1?
check.a: That value may already have been chosen, and safety requires never choosing a different one.

raft-consensus-for-humans.core: Raft was designed for understandability. It decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication and safety, uses a strong leader (all writes go through it) and terms (logical epochs) to detect stale leaders. It's used by etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV and Kafka's KRaft.

first_principles.problem: Engineers struggle to implement and reason about Paxos correctly.
truths: Understandable designs are implemented correctly more often.

analogy.title: A classroom with a single elected class monitor
analogy.story: The monitor records decisions; if they're absent too long, a new election is held.
analogy.breaks: Class monitors serve a term length; Raft leaders serve until they fail or lose contact.

check.a: A monotonically increasing logical period, each starting with an election, used to detect stale leaders.

raft-concept-1-leader-election.core: Followers expect heartbeats from the leader. If none arrives within a randomised election timeout (e.g. 150–300 ms), a follower becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and requests votes. Nodes grant one vote per term, only to candidates whose log is at least as up to date. A majority wins; randomisation prevents repeated split votes.

first_principles.problem: Two followers time out simultaneously, split the vote and no leader emerges.
truths: One vote per term prevents double leaders.
derivation: **Vote once per term**, only for up-to-date logs.
**Majority** wins; higher term deposes old leaders.

analogy.title: A group choosing a new leader when the old one goes quiet
analogy.story: The first person to notice, at a slightly random moment, asks for votes, which avoids everyone shouting at once.
analogy.breaks: People recognise each other's knowledge; Raft compares log index and term explicitly.

example.title: Election trace
flow: Node B times out at 210 ms → term 4 candidate
A and C grant votes (B's log up to date)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: New leader in a few hundred ms.

check.q: Why are Raft election timeouts randomised?
check.a: To make simultaneous candidacies and split votes unlikely.

raft-concept-2-log-replication.core: The leader appends client commands to its log and sends AppendEntries with the previous entry's index and term. Followers accept only if they have that previous entry (log matching), otherwise the leader backs up and retries. An entry is committed once stored on a majority (from the current term), and then every node applies committed entries to its state machine in order.

first_principles.problem: A follower missed several entries during a network blip and its log diverged from the leader's.
truths: Logs must be identical up to the commit index.

analogy.title: A teacher dictating notes
analogy.story: Before each new line, students confirm they wrote the previous one correctly; if not, the teacher goes back.
analogy.breaks: Students keep their own notes; Raft followers' conflicting entries are overwritten by the leader.

example.title: Repairing a follower
flow: Leader sends entry 9 with prev (8, term 4) → reject
Leader backs up to index 6 → accept

check.q: When is a Raft log entry considered committed?
check.a: When the leader has replicated an entry from its current term to a majority of nodes.

zab-zookeeper-atomic-broadcast.core: ZooKeeper uses Zab: a leader-based atomic broadcast protocol guaranteeing that state changes are delivered in the same total order to all servers, with a recovery phase on leader change that synchronises followers to the new leader's history before new proposals. Transaction IDs (zxid) combine epoch and counter, similar to Raft's term and index.

first_principles.problem: Teams use ZooKeeper but don't know how it keeps ordering through leader failures.
truths: Primary-backup ordering needs a single leader.
Leader changes must not lose committed state.

analogy.title: A news agency's single editor-in-chief
analogy.story: Every story is published in one order; a new editor first reviews everything already published before continuing.
analogy.breaks: Editors choose stories; Zab leaders must preserve every committed proposal.

example.title: Leader change
flow: New leader elected with highest zxid

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No committed change lost or reordered.

check.q: What does a ZooKeeper zxid consist of?
check.a: An epoch (leader generation) and a counter within that epoch.

the-danger-split-brain-scenarios.core: Split-brain occurs when two nodes both believe they're the leader and accept conflicting writes, typically after a partition or a paused (GC, VM freeze) old leader that wakes up. Consensus prevents it with majority quorums and terms: an old leader can't get a majority and is rejected for its stale term. External systems need fencing tokens to reject stale leaders' actions.

first_principles.problem: An old leader paused by a 30-second GC wakes up and writes to storage after a new leader took over.
truths: Nodes can't tell they've been paused.
Majorities can only exist on one side.
Stale authority must be rejected by resources.
derivation: Use **leader leases** carefully with clock bounds.

analogy.title: Two captains issuing orders to the same crew
analogy.story: Chaos follows unless orders carry a rank that crews check.
analogy.breaks: Crews can see both captains; systems may not know a second leader exists.

example.title: Fencing token
flow: Paused; new leader term 8 gets token 8, writes
Old leader wakes, writes with token 7

check.q: How does a fencing token prevent split-brain damage?
check.a: Resources reject operations carrying a token older than the highest they've seen, blocking stale leaders.

practical-considerations-timeouts-perfor.core: Running consensus in production means tuning election timeouts above network RTT and disk latency but low enough for fast failover, batching and pipelining log entries for throughput, keeping members in nearby zones (every commit waits for a majority round trip), snapshotting to bound log size, and changing membership safely (one node at a time or joint consensus, learners first).

first_principles.problem: A five-region Raft group commits slowly, and adding nodes carelessly breaks quorum.
derivation: Change membership **one at a time** or **joint consensus**; use **learners**.

analogy.title: Running a committee across time zones
analogy.story: Meetings are slow when members are far apart, and adding members changes how many votes you need.
analogy.breaks: Committees can vote asynchronously by email; Raft commits always wait for a majority ack.

example.title: Latency budget
flow: 3 voters in one region across AZs: commit ~2 ms
Use regional groups + async replication across regions

check.q: Why do geographically spread Raft groups commit slowly?
check.a: Every commit waits for acknowledgements from a majority, so latency to the nearest majority dominates.
